summary.text: Uranium-235 is an isotope making up about 0.72% of natural uranium and, unlike the more common uranium-238, it is fissile.
Fissile means it can sustain a nuclear chain reaction, and its fission powers most nuclear reactors and nuclear weapons.
Making fuel or weapons often needs uranium enrichment, a process that raises the proportion of uranium-235 in natural uranium.

facts.label: Neutrons per fission
facts.value: An average of 2.43, most often two or three

items.prompt: Natural uranium is mostly uranium-238, but uranium-235 matters most for energy. What can it do that uranium-238 cannot?

options.label: Give off no radiation at all
Sustain a nuclear chain reaction
Dissolve in ordinary water
Exist in nature as a free element

items.explain: Unlike the predominant isotope uranium-238, uranium-235 is fissile, meaning it can sustain a nuclear chain reaction.

items.prompt: A uranium-235 nucleus splits and releases two or three neutrons. What has to happen for the reaction to keep itself going?

options.label: All the neutrons must escape the fuel
Every neutron must split a new nucleus
The fuel must be cooled to near zero
At least one neutron must hit another nucleus and split it

items.explain: If at least one neutron from a fission strikes another nucleus and causes it to fission, the chain reaction continues.

items.prompt: Operators of a reactor want to change its power output. How do they adjust it?

options.label: Move neutron-absorbing rods in or out of the core
Add more uranium-238 to the fuel
Change the half-life of the fuel
Cool the fuel below critical mass

items.explain: Power output is adjusted by the location of control rods containing elements that strongly absorb neutrons, such as boron, cadmium or hafnium.

items.prompt: A reactor uses fuel with only a little uranium-235 and still keeps a chain reaction going. What makes that possible?

options.label: Speeding the neutrons up so they hit harder
Cooling the uranium until it turns fissile
Slowing the neutrons, since slow ones split nuclei more readily
Adding uranium-238 to absorb stray neutrons

items.explain: A critical chain reaction can be achieved at low concentrations if fission neutrons are moderated to lower their speed, since fission is more probable with slow neutrons.

items.prompt: Some reactors run on natural uranium, but light water reactors cannot. What forces them to use enriched fuel?

options.label: Light water reacts chemically with uranium-238
Light water absorbs neutrons more strongly
Light water slows fission to nothing
Light water makes the fuel too hot

items.explain: Light water reactors must use low enriched uranium because of the higher neutron absorption of light water.

items.prompt: Uranium-235 declines relative to uranium-238 over billions of years. What can scientists do with how that ratio started and where it is now?

options.label: Measure how much fuel remains underground
Work out how quickly a bomb would fizzle
Tell which ores contain gold
Estimate the time since modern uranium nuclei were formed

items.explain: Knowledge of the production and present ratios of uranium-235 to uranium-238 allows radiometric dating of the time since modern uranium nuclei were formed.
